standard.title: Language shapes relationships and roles
standard.description: recognise how language shapes relationships and roles
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can understand how language is used to build relationships and how word choices affect how ideas are perceived (AC9E7LA01). They have not yet examined how language actively constructs group identity, solidarity, and role differentiation through shared terminology and address forms.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise how language choices shape relationships between people and define social roles, including how shared language features create group solidarity.

nodes.label: Language and group identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language features — such as specialist terminology, acronyms and terms of address — that signal group membership and create solidarity.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two language features (e.g. specialist terms, forms of address) in one text or social context that signal group membership.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and explain how language features including specialist terminology, acronyms and terms of address create solidarity and define group identity across several social and cultural contexts, including examples from youth culture, sport or professional communities.
wider: Investigate how First Nations language names (such as those on the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia) reflect relationships to Country/Place and construct group and community identity
Compare how two contrasting groups (e.g. a sporting team and a professional workplace) use language differently to signal membership and manage relationships
Examine how language associated with a particular online community or subculture both includes insiders and excludes outsiders

response_modes.reason: Students may over-generalise from a single example (e.g. only sports contexts). Encountering diverse groups — youth culture, workplace, First Nations communities — builds a more robust understanding that this is a universal language function, not context-specific.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The diversity of group contexts available — sport, profession, youth culture, First Nations language communities — provides rich cross-contextual comparison that deepens the concept well beyond minimum recognition.
success_criteria: Identifies specific language features (specialist terms, acronyms, terms of address) in a given text and names the group they are associated with.
Explains how at least one identified language feature creates a sense of belonging or shared identity among group members.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who over-generalise from a single group context arrive at Node 2 without the pluralised understanding that language functions this way across all social groups. Node 2's conceptual shift — from language reflecting roles to language constructing them — cannot be made without encountering how this mechanism operates in varied group contexts.

nodes.label: Language constructing roles and relationships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise how language choices position people in roles (e.g. leader, peer, outsider) and shape the nature of relationships between individuals and groups.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how one text uses language (e.g. forms of address, inclusive/exclusive pronouns, tone) to define a role or relationship between at least two parties.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how language choices — including word selection, tone, inclusive/exclusive language and forms of address — construct roles and power relationships across a range of text types including informal conversation, formal speech and social media.
wider: Analyse how language use in a text positions one group as dominant or authoritative relative to another, considering implicit and explicit role markers
Investigate how the same individual uses different language choices to construct different roles in different contexts (e.g. a public figure speaking formally vs informally)
Explore how language choices in First Nations contexts reflect distinct relational and role structures that differ from mainstream Australian English conventions

response_modes.reason: The shift from 'language reflects roles' to 'language constructs roles' is a subtle conceptual move students often miss. Scaffolding the reasoning — showing how the same event can be described in ways that create very different power dynamics — helps students see language as constitutive, not merely reflective.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one specific language choice in a text and explains how it positions a person in a particular role or relationship.
Uses appropriate metalanguage (e.g. 'forms of address', 'inclusive pronoun', 'tone') when discussing how language shapes relationships.
